notes.front: What is the standard atmosphere, in one sentence?
notes.back: An agreed reference atmosphere: at sea level, pressure 29.92 inches of mercury and temperature 15 °C (59 °F).
notes.explanation: Most aircraft performance data assume these standard conditions, so real conditions are compared against them.
notes.example: A 30 °C sea-level afternoon is 15 °C warmer than standard, so aircraft perform worse than their book figures.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Measurement of Atmosphere Pressure”, p. 22

notes.front: What is density altitude, in one sentence?
notes.back: The altitude in the standard atmosphere that has the same air density as the air you are actually in.
notes.explanation: It measures how ‘thin’ the air feels to the aircraft: the higher the density altitude, the worse the performance.
notes.example: A hot afternoon at a 5,000 ft site can leave a drone flying as if it were thousands of feet higher.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Density Altitude”, p. 21

notes.front: What is (relative) humidity?
notes.back: The amount of water vapour in the air, as a percentage of the most the air could hold at that temperature.
notes.explanation: Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air; saturated air is at 100%.
notes.example: Perfectly dry air is at 0%; saturated air that can hold no more water vapour is at 100%.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Effects of Humidity (Moisture) on Density”, p. 22

notes.front: What are convective currents?
notes.back: Small local circulations of rising and sinking air, caused by uneven heating of different surfaces.
notes.explanation: They make the air bumpy and can upset a small aircraft’s control near the ground.
notes.example: Air rising off a sunny car park next to a cool lake.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.4.2, p. B-2

notes.front: What is wind shear?
notes.back: A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area.
notes.explanation: It can throw an aircraft up or down and change its speed abruptly; near the ground there is little room to recover.
notes.example: A steady headwind that turns into a tailwind within seconds as you climb.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 23

notes.front: What is a microburst?
notes.back: The most severe type of low-level wind shear: a small, short-lived area of intense downdraft linked to rain from a shower or storm.
notes.explanation: It forms when rain from a shower or storm falls into dry air at the cloud base, and can produce downdrafts of up to 6,000 feet per minute.
notes.example: Under a shower from a building storm, a ring of blowing dust on the ground can be the only visible clue.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 24

notes.front: What is atmospheric stability?
notes.back: The atmosphere’s ability to resist vertical motion: stable air damps out up-and-down movement; unstable air lets it grow.
notes.explanation: Stability decides whether you get smooth, hazy, layered weather or bumpy air, towering clouds and storms.
notes.example: A calm grey morning under a flat cloud layer is stable air; a summer afternoon of towering clouds is unstable.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Atmospheric Stability”, p. 24

notes.front: What is a temperature inversion?
notes.back: A layer in which air temperature rises with altitude, instead of falling as usual.
notes.explanation: The warm top acts as a lid, trapping weather and pollutants beneath it.
notes.example: On a clear, still night the ground cools the air just above it, so the air a few hundred feet up is warmer.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Inversion”, p. 24

notes.front: What is frost, in weather terms?
notes.back: Ice deposited on surfaces when they cool below the dew point and the temperature is below freezing.
notes.explanation: Dew is harmless to a small UA, but frost is a definite flight-safety hazard.
notes.example: After a clear, calm, cold night, a drone left outside has frost on its propellers.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Dew and Frost”, p. 25

notes.front: What is an air mass?
notes.back: A large body of air that has taken on the temperature and moisture of the region where it formed.
notes.explanation: Its source decides whether it brings cold or warm, dry or moist air, and so the weather it carries.
notes.example: A continental polar air mass brings cool, dry air; a maritime tropical one brings warm, moist air.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Air Masses”, p. 12-17

notes.front: What is a front?
notes.back: The boundary between two air masses of different characteristics.
notes.explanation: Temperature, humidity and wind often change quickly across it, so an approaching front means the weather is about to change.
notes.example: A cold front passing through brings a sudden wind shift, showers and then clearer, cooler air.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fronts”, p. 12-18

notes.front: What is a thunderstorm, as a weather hazard?
notes.back: A cumulonimbus cloud system with strong updrafts and downdrafts that can produce heavy rain, hail, lightning, tornadoes and wind shear.
notes.explanation: Pilots treat the cumulonimbus as perhaps the most dangerous cloud type.
notes.example: A towering anvil-topped cloud on a summer afternoon.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Clouds”, p. 25

notes.front: What is a squall line?
notes.back: A narrow band of active thunderstorms, often on or ahead of a cold front in moist, unstable air.
notes.explanation: It can be too long to go around and too severe to go through.
notes.example: A line of storms stretching across several counties late on a hot afternoon.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Squall Line”, p. 12-23

notes.front: What is structural icing?
notes.back: Ice that forms on the aircraft itself in flight when it flies through visible moisture at 0 °C or colder.
notes.explanation: Like frost, ice on lifting surfaces disturbs the airflow; icing in thunderstorms can be extremely hazardous.
notes.example: Freezing drizzle glazing a drone’s propellers on a cold, grey day.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Structural Icing”, p. 26; Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Icing”

notes.front: What is fog?
notes.back: A cloud on the surface, usually formed when the air near the ground cools to its dew point.
notes.explanation: It reduces visibility at the surface, sometimes below part 107’s 3 SM minimum.
notes.example: Morning fog filling a valley after a clear, still night.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-15

notes.front: What are standard sea-level pressure and temperature?
notes.back: 29.92 inches of mercury (1,013.2 mb) and 15 °C (59 °F).
notes.explanation: These are the basis for most aircraft performance data.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Measurement of Atmosphere Pressure”, p. 22

notes.front: Roughly how much does atmospheric pressure fall per 1,000 ft of height near the ground?
notes.back: About 1 inch of mercury per 1,000 ft.
notes.explanation: Stations use this to convert their readings to sea-level pressure for reports.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Measurement of Atmosphere Pressure”, p. 22

notes.front: What does a high density altitude mean for aircraft performance?
notes.back: The air is thin, so performance decreases.
notes.explanation: Lower density altitude (denser air) gives better performance.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Density Altitude”, p. 21

notes.front: As air temperature rises, what happens to density altitude?
notes.back: It rises: warmer air is less dense.
notes.explanation: At constant pressure, density varies inversely with temperature.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Density Altitude”, p. 21

notes.front: As atmospheric pressure falls, what happens to density altitude?
notes.back: It rises: lower pressure means less dense air.
notes.explanation: At constant temperature, density is directly proportional to pressure.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Density Altitude”, p. 21

notes.front: How does a higher site elevation affect density altitude?
notes.back: Higher elevation gives a higher density altitude.
notes.explanation: Pressure falls quickly with height and usually outweighs the cooling, so air density decreases with altitude.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Density Altitude”, p. 21

notes.front: How does higher humidity affect density altitude, and why?
notes.back: It raises density altitude: water vapour is lighter than air, so moist air is less dense.
notes.explanation: Humidity alone is usually a minor, contributing factor compared with temperature and pressure.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Effects of Humidity (Moisture) on Density”, p. 22

notes.front: When does an AWOS add density altitude to its report?
notes.back: When density altitude is more than 1,000 ft above the field elevation.
notes.explanation: AWOS-1 and higher levels also include a density altitude figure in their reports.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual (Basic with Change 3, 9 July 2026), para. 7-1-10, “Weather Observing Programs”

notes.front: Figure: density altitude chart. Follow the ‘Sea level’ line to the right, towards warmer temperatures. What happens to density altitude?
notes.back: It rises above sea level: the warmer the air, the higher the density altitude.
notes.explanation: Every pressure-altitude line slopes upward to the right, showing temperature raising density altitude.
notes.source: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 8

notes.front: Figure: density altitude chart. In the table, which altimeter setting has a conversion factor of 0, and what do lower settings do?
notes.back: 29.92 inHg, standard pressure. Lower settings give positive factors: add them to get a higher pressure altitude, and so higher density altitude.
notes.explanation: 29.92 inHg is standard sea-level pressure, so it needs no correction.
notes.source: FAA, Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 8

notes.front: A station 5,000 ft above sea level reads 24.92 inches of mercury. What sea-level pressure does it report?
notes.back: 29.92 inches of mercury, standard.
notes.explanation: Stations add about 1 inHg per 1,000 ft of elevation to convert to sea level.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Measurement of Atmosphere Pressure”, p. 23

notes.front: Which site gives the higher density altitude: a coastal field at dawn in winter, or a 6,000 ft mountain site on a hot, humid afternoon?
notes.back: The hot, humid mountain site.
notes.choices:
A) The coastal field at dawn in winter
B) The mountain site on a hot, humid afternoon
C) They are the same, because density altitude depends only on elevation
notes.choicesExplained: A: low elevation, cold air and dry air all give a low density altitude. C: temperature, pressure and humidity also change density altitude.
notes.explanation: High elevation, high temperature and high humidity all raise density altitude, reducing performance.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Density Altitude”, p. 21

notes.front: Two sites share the same elevation, temperature and pressure; one is humid, the other dry. Which has the higher density altitude?
notes.back: The humid site.
notes.explanation: Water vapour is lighter than air, so moist air is less dense, raising density altitude and reducing performance a little.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Effects of Humidity (Moisture) on Density”, p. 22

notes.front: What do buildings, trees and rough terrain do to the wind near the ground?
notes.back: They break up its flow, creating gusts that change rapidly in direction and speed.
notes.explanation: Be vigilant near large buildings, other structures and natural obstructions such as bluffs and canyons.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.4.1, p. B-2

notes.front: What decides how turbulent the air around a ground obstruction is?
notes.back: The size of the obstruction and the basic speed of the wind.
notes.explanation: Bigger obstacles and stronger winds give worse turbulence.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Effect of Obstructions on Wind”, p. 23

notes.front: When wind blows across a mountain or ridge, on which side is the air turbulent, and what can it do to an aircraft?
notes.back: The leeward (downwind) side: descending, turbulent air can push an aircraft into the slope.
notes.explanation: The windward side has smooth upward flow; the stronger the wind, the worse the lee-side downdraft. Downdrafts in valleys and canyons can be severe.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.4.1, p. B-2

notes.front: Over mountains, what do winds above 25 knots and above 40 knots at mountain-top level suggest?
notes.back: Above 25 knots: some turbulence. Above 40 knots across a barrier: caution is needed.
notes.explanation: Stratified clouds mean stable air; convective clouds on the windward side mean unstable air.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Mountain Flying”, p. 26

notes.front: What do standing lenticular clouds indicate?
notes.back: A mountain wave (waves in the wind flow downwind of a mountain barrier) with very strong turbulence; avoid them.
notes.explanation: They form on wave crests downwind of barriers, look smooth-edged and barely move, though strong wind blows through them.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Standing Lenticular Altocumulus Clouds”, p. 25; p. 26, “Mountain Flying”

notes.front: Which surfaces give off the most heat, and which absorb and keep it?
notes.back: Ploughed ground, rock, sand and barren land give off more; water, trees and other vegetation absorb and retain it.
notes.explanation: The uneven heating creates convective currents.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.4.2, p. B-2

notes.front: On a sunny afternoon your drone crosses from a hot sand quarry to a lake and suddenly bounces. What is the likely cause?
notes.back: Convective currents from the uneven heating of sand and water.
notes.explanation: Rising and sinking air over different surfaces makes bumpy air that can affect controllability.
notes.source: FAA, AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶B.4.2, p. B-2

notes.front: You inspect the downwind face of a large warehouse on a windy day. What wind should you expect?
notes.back: Turbulent, rapidly changing gusts, stronger the bigger the building and the stronger the wind.
notes.explanation: Buildings break up the wind’s flow near the ground.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Effect of Obstructions on Wind”, p. 23

notes.front: Which weather systems commonly bring low-level wind shear?
notes.back: Passing fronts and thunderstorms.
notes.explanation: It is also associated with temperature inversions and strong upper-level winds over 25 knots.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 23

notes.front: What happens to performance when a headwind suddenly changes to a tailwind?
notes.back: Airspeed and performance decrease.
notes.explanation: The opposite change, tailwind to headwind, briefly increases them; either way the pilot must react at once.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 24

notes.front: How big is a typical microburst?
notes.back: About 1–2 miles across and about 1,000 ft deep.
notes.explanation: Its small size means it can surprise an aircraft that was in calm air moments before.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 24

notes.front: How long does a microburst last, and how strong can its downdrafts be?
notes.back: About 5–15 minutes, with downdrafts of up to 6,000 feet per minute.
notes.explanation: It can also cause headwind losses of 30–90 knots and strong turbulence.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 24

notes.front: In what order does an aircraft flying through a microburst meet its winds?
notes.back: First a headwind, then a downdraft, then a rapidly increasing tailwind.
notes.explanation: The sequence can drive an aircraft into the ground.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 24

notes.front: What visual clues can point to a microburst?
notes.back: An intense rain shaft at the surface with virga at the cloud base, or a ring of blowing dust.
notes.explanation: Virga is rain that evaporates before reaching the ground.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 24

notes.front: Your drone, flying into wind near a storm, suddenly gains lift and climbs, then is pushed sharply down. What is likely next?
notes.back: A strong tailwind as it exits a microburst; land or leave the area at once.
notes.explanation: Microbursts give a headwind, then a downdraft, then a rapidly increasing tailwind.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 24

notes.front: A cold front is passing through your area this afternoon. Which low-level wind hazard should you plan for?
notes.back: Wind shear: sudden changes in wind speed and direction near the ground.
notes.explanation: Low-level wind shear is commonly associated with passing fronts.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 23

notes.front: Which air is most stable, and which most unstable?
notes.back: Cool, dry air is very stable; warm, moist air is the most unstable.
notes.explanation: That is why tropical summers bring daily thunderstorms.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Atmospheric Stability”, p. 24

notes.front: Unstable versus stable air: what clouds does each typically bring?
notes.back: Unstable: cumuliform clouds. Stable: stratiform clouds and fog.
notes.explanation: Stability determines an air mass’s typical weather.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Stability”, p. 26

notes.front: Unstable versus stable air: what precipitation does each typically bring?
notes.back: Unstable: showery precipitation. Stable: continuous precipitation.
notes.explanation: Stability determines an air mass’s typical weather.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Stability”, p. 26

notes.front: Unstable versus stable air: what air (turbulence) does each typically bring?
notes.back: Unstable: rough, turbulent air. Stable: smooth air.
notes.explanation: Stability determines an air mass’s typical weather.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Stability”, p. 26

notes.front: Unstable versus stable air: what visibility does each typically bring?
notes.back: Unstable: good visibility, except in blowing obstructions. Stable: fair to poor visibility in haze and smoke.
notes.explanation: Stability determines an air mass’s typical weather.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Stability”, p. 26

notes.front: A forecast gives towering cumulus, showers and bumpy air with good visibility. Stable or unstable air?
notes.back: Unstable air.
notes.explanation: Cumuliform clouds, showery precipitation, turbulence and good visibility are the marks of instability.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Stability”, p. 26

notes.front: A morning with a flat grey cloud layer, steady drizzle, smooth air and haze. Stable or unstable air?
notes.back: Stable air.
notes.explanation: Stratiform clouds, continuous precipitation, smooth air and poor visibility mark stable air.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Stability”, p. 26

notes.front: What can a temperature inversion trap near the ground?
notes.back: Weather and pollutants; with high humidity, fog, haze, smoke or low cloud, reducing visibility.
notes.explanation: Inversion layers are usually shallow layers of smooth, stable air near the ground.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Inversion”, p. 24

notes.front: When do surface-based temperature inversions form?
notes.back: On clear, cool nights, when the cold ground cools the air just above it.
notes.explanation: Frontal inversions form where warm air spreads over cooler air.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Inversion”, p. 24

notes.front: After a clear, calm night, a valley site is hazy and smoky under clear skies above. What explains it?
notes.back: A surface-based temperature inversion trapping haze and smoke near the ground.
notes.explanation: The warmer layer above acts as a lid on the cooler air beneath.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Inversion”, p. 24

notes.front: What happens when air cools to its dew point?
notes.back: It becomes saturated, and moisture condenses as fog, dew, frost, cloud, rain or snow.
notes.explanation: The dew point is the temperature at which the air can hold no more moisture.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Temperature/Dew Point Relationship”, p. 25

notes.front: What does a small spread between temperature and dew point warn of?
notes.back: Fog, low clouds and precipitation are highly likely.
notes.explanation: The closer the two figures, the nearer the air is to saturation.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Methods by Which Air Reaches the Saturation Point”, p. 25

notes.front: What are two of the four ways air can reach its saturation point?
notes.back: Any two of: warm air moving over a cold surface; cold and warm air mixing; air cooling at night on cold ground; air being lifted.
notes.explanation: Each cools the air or adds moisture until temperature meets dew point.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Methods by Which Air Reaches the Saturation Point”, p. 25

notes.front: Why must frost be removed before flight?
notes.back: It disrupts airflow over lifting surfaces, reducing lift and increasing drag.
notes.explanation: Together these can stop an aircraft taking off safely, so clean it thoroughly first.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Dew and Frost”, p. 25

notes.front: After a clear, calm night below freezing, your drone’s propellers have a thin white coating. What should you do?
notes.back: Remove all the frost before flight.
notes.explanation: Frost reduces lift and increases drag; a small UA must be free of frost before flight.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Dew and Frost”, p. 25

notes.front: How are air masses classified?
notes.back: Polar or tropical by temperature, and maritime or continental by moisture.
notes.explanation: So a maritime tropical air mass is warm and moist; a continental polar one cool and dry.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Air Masses”, p. 12-17

notes.front: What happens to an air mass moving over a warmer surface?
notes.back: It is heated from below and becomes unstable: cumulus, showers, turbulence, but good surface visibility.
notes.explanation: Convective currents form as the lower air warms and rises.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Air Masses”, p. 12-18

notes.front: What happens to an air mass moving over a colder surface?
notes.back: It becomes stable, with poor surface visibility; it can produce low stratus and fog.
notes.explanation: Smoke and dust cannot rise out of stable air, so they stay trapped near the surface.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Air Masses”, p. 12-18

notes.front: A cold, dry air mass flows over much warmer ground on a spring afternoon. Will it become stable or unstable, and what weather follows?
notes.back: Unstable: cumulus clouds, showers and turbulence, with good surface visibility.
notes.explanation: An air mass heated from below develops convective currents and becomes unstable.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Air Masses”, p. 12-18

notes.front: What does an approaching front of any type mean?
notes.back: A change in the weather is imminent.
notes.explanation: Across a front, temperature, humidity and wind often change rapidly over short distances.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fronts”, p. 12-18

notes.front: What is a warm front, and what weather usually comes before it?
notes.back: Warm air advancing over colder air; slow-moving, with stratiform or cirriform clouds and fog ahead of it.
notes.explanation: Warm fronts move at about 10–25 mph; in summer, thunderstorms are likely to develop.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Warm Front”, p. 12-18

notes.front: What is a cold front, and what weather comes with it?
notes.back: Cold air replacing warmer air; faster-moving, with towering cumulus or cumulonimbus, showers, gusty winds and poor visibility.
notes.explanation: The PHAK gives cold-front speeds of about 25–30 mph, and elsewhere 20–35 mph; after passage the sky clears quickly.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Cold Front”, p. 12-20

notes.front: What is a stationary front?
notes.back: A front between two air masses of roughly equal force, so it does not move; mixed weather can persist for days.
notes.explanation: Its weather is typically a mixture of warm-front and cold-front weather.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Stationary Front”, p. 12-21

notes.front: What is an occluded front?
notes.back: A fast-moving cold front that has caught up with a slow-moving warm front.
notes.explanation: As it approaches, warm-front weather comes first, followed immediately by cold-front weather.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Occluded Front”, p. 12-21

notes.front: Towering cumulus, heavy showers and gusty, variable winds arrive, then within hours the sky clears and it turns cooler. Which front passed?
notes.back: A cold front.
notes.explanation: Cold fronts bring rapid, complete weather changes and clear quickly behind them.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Cold Front”, p. 12-20

notes.front: Warm front versus cold front: which gives advance warning, and which arrives with little warning?
notes.back: Warm fronts give advance warning and pass slowly; cold fronts arrive fast with little warning and change the weather within hours.
notes.explanation: Warm fronts can take days to pass; cold-front weather clears rapidly behind the front.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Comparison of Cold and Warm Fronts”, p. 12-21

notes.front: Which three ingredients does a thunderstorm need?
notes.back: Sufficient water vapour, an unstable lapse rate (unstable air), and an initial lifting action.
notes.explanation: Surface heating, fronts, converging winds or mountains can supply the lift.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Thunderstorms”, p. 12-23

notes.front: What is the key feature of a thunderstorm’s cumulus stage?
notes.back: Updrafts, which build the cloud; its growth can exceed 3,000 feet per minute.
notes.explanation: Every thunderstorm begins as a cumulus, though most cumulus never become storms.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Thunderstorm Life Cycle”, p. 26

notes.front: What signals that a thunderstorm has entered its mature stage?
notes.back: Precipitation starting to fall from the cloud base, showing that a downdraft has formed.
notes.explanation: Updrafts and downdrafts side by side create strong shear and turbulence.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Thunderstorm Life Cycle”, p. 27

notes.front: In which stage are all thunderstorm hazards at their greatest intensity?
notes.back: The mature stage.
notes.explanation: Its down-rushing air also spreads out at the surface as strong, gusty winds, the leading edge being the ‘first gust’.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Thunderstorm Life Cycle”, p. 27

notes.front: What characterises a thunderstorm’s dissipating stage?
notes.back: Downdrafts; the storm dies rapidly.
notes.explanation: When the rain ends and the downdrafts weaken, only harmless cloud remnants remain.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Thunderstorm Life Cycle”, p. 27

notes.front: How far should you stay from a thunderstorm identified as severe, and why?
notes.back: At least 20 NM, because hail may fall for miles outside the cloud.
notes.explanation: If going around is not possible, stay on the ground until it passes.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Thunderstorms”, p. 12-23

notes.front: How strong can the updrafts and downdrafts in a thunderstorm be?
notes.back: Over 3,000 feet per minute; in a mature storm, updrafts may exceed 6,000 feet per minute.
notes.explanation: They make a thunderstorm no place for a small UA.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Clouds”, p. 25

notes.front: Why is a squall line so dangerous?
notes.back: It is often the single most intense weather hazard to aircraft, and may be too long to detour and too severe to penetrate.
notes.explanation: It usually forms rapidly and peaks in the late afternoon and first hours of darkness.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Squall Line”, p. 12-23

notes.front: Where can hail from a thunderstorm be met?
notes.back: Under and near the storm, and even in clear air several miles away; rain at the surface doesn’t rule out hail aloft.
notes.explanation: Expect hail with any thunderstorm, especially beneath the anvil of a large cumulonimbus.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Hail”, p. 12-24

notes.front: What separates a funnel cloud, a tornado and a waterspout?
notes.back: A funnel cloud does not reach the surface; a tornado touches land; a waterspout touches water.
notes.explanation: Tornado winds are estimated to exceed 200 knots; any cloud connected to a severe thunderstorm carries a threat of violence.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Tornadoes”, p. 12-23

notes.front: What damage can a lightning strike do to an aircraft?
notes.back: It can puncture the skin and damage communication and electronic navigation equipment.
notes.explanation: Severe storms, as a rule, have a high frequency of lightning.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Lightning”, p. 12-25

notes.front: A cumulus cloud near your site is growing fast, and now rain starts falling from its base. Which stage is it in, and what should you do?
notes.back: The mature stage, when all hazards peak; land and wait for the storm to pass.
notes.explanation: Precipitation from the base means a downdraft has formed, bringing gusty winds and possible hail and lightning.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Thunderstorm Life Cycle”, p. 27

notes.front: A storm cloud is producing only downdrafts, and its rain is easing. Which stage is it in?
notes.back: The dissipating stage.
notes.explanation: Downdrafts characterise dissipation; updrafts mark the cumulus stage, and both together the mature stage.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Thunderstorm Life Cycle”, p. 27

notes.front: A thunderstorm is 5 miles away, but the sky above your site is clear. Are you safe from hail?
notes.back: No. Hail can fall in clear air several miles from the storm.
notes.explanation: The advice is to keep at least 20 NM from severe thunderstorms.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Hail”, p. 12-24

notes.front: Which two conditions are needed for structural icing in flight?
notes.back: Visible moisture (rain or cloud droplets), and a temperature of 0 °C or colder where the moisture strikes the aircraft.
notes.explanation: Be alert for icing whenever the temperature approaches 0 °C and visible moisture is present.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Structural Icing”, p. 26; Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Icing”

notes.front: Can structural icing form when the air is a few degrees above 0 °C?
notes.back: Yes: aerodynamic cooling can lower a lifting surface to 0 °C even when the air is slightly warmer.
notes.explanation: So do not treat +1 °C or +2 °C in visible moisture as safe.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Structural Icing”, p. 26

notes.front: It is drizzling at +1 °C. Is there any risk of structural icing on your drone?
notes.back: Yes: there is visible moisture, and aerodynamic cooling can bring surfaces to 0 °C.
notes.explanation: Both conditions for icing may be met even though the air is just above freezing.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Structural Icing”, p. 26

notes.front: Which fog forms on clear nights with little or no wind, usually in low-lying areas, and burns off as the sun rises?
notes.back: Radiation fog.
notes.explanation: The ground cools quickly by radiation until the air above reaches its dew point; wind also speeds its clearing.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-15

notes.front: What is ground fog?
notes.back: Radiation fog less than 20 ft thick.
notes.explanation: It is the shallowest form of radiation fog.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-15

notes.front: Which fog forms when warm, moist air moves over a colder surface, as along coasts?
notes.back: Advection fog.
notes.explanation: Unlike radiation fog, it needs wind to form.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-16

notes.front: How does wind speed affect advection fog?
notes.back: Winds of up to 15 knots let it form and thicken; above 15 knots it usually lifts into low stratus cloud.
notes.explanation: Sea breezes carrying moist air over cooler land make it common on coasts.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-16

notes.front: Which fog forms when moist, stable air is forced up sloping ground such as a mountain range?
notes.back: Upslope fog.
notes.explanation: Like advection fog, it needs wind to form and to continue.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-16

notes.front: Which fog forms when cold, dry air moves over warm water, and which hazards come with it?
notes.back: Steam fog (sea smoke); low-level turbulence and icing are commonly associated with it.
notes.explanation: It is common over bodies of water in the coldest times of year.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-16

notes.front: When does ice fog form?
notes.back: In very cold weather, usually −25 °F or colder, when water vapour turns directly into ice crystals.
notes.explanation: It is mostly an arctic phenomenon but can occur in middle latitudes in the cold season.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-16

notes.front: Radiation fog versus advection and upslope fog: which usually burns off with the morning sun?
notes.back: Radiation fog burns off; advection and upslope fog may persist for days and extend higher.
notes.explanation: Advection and upslope fog both need wind to form and continue, unlike radiation fog.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-16

notes.front: On a cold winter morning, a warm, moist sea breeze drifts over cold coastal farmland at 10 knots and fog forms. Which type?
notes.back: Advection fog.
notes.explanation: Warm, moist air moving over a colder surface, with light wind, forms advection fog.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-16

notes.front: After a clear, windless night, a river valley is full of fog at dawn. What is likely to happen as the morning goes on?
notes.back: It is radiation fog, which should lift and burn off as the sun warms the ground, faster if the wind picks up.
notes.explanation: Plan to wait until visibility meets part 107’s 3 SM minimum.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 12, “Fog”, p. 12-15

notes.front: In weather reports, what does visibility mean?
notes.back: The greatest horizontal distance at which prominent objects can be seen with the naked eye.
notes.explanation: It is reported in METARs and by automated stations, and forecast in briefings.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Visibility”, p. 28

notes.front: The METAR shows 2SM BR, and your site is next to the airport. May you fly under part 107?
notes.back: No: visibility is 2 SM, below the 3 SM part 107 minimum.
notes.explanation: Mist (BR) is an obscuration that reduces visibility.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.51, “Operating limitations for small unmanned aircraft” (eCFR, current as of 2026-09-25)
uses: weather codes (VC, TS, SH, FZ, RA, GR, FC, BR, FG, HZ, FU)

notes.front: What does a steadily rising barometric pressure usually indicate, and a rapidly falling one?
notes.back: Rising: fair weather approaching. Falling, especially rapidly: bad weather and possibly severe storms.
notes.explanation: Forecasters track pressure trends to predict how weather systems will move.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Measurement of Atmosphere Pressure”, p. 23

notes.front: High density altitude versus low density altitude: which comes with thin air and poor performance?
notes.back: High density altitude: thin air, poorer performance. Low density altitude: dense air, better performance.
notes.explanation: High elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity all push density altitude up.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Density Altitude”, p. 21

notes.front: Dew versus frost: when does each form, and which is a flight hazard?
notes.back: Both form when surfaces cool below the dew point; frost forms when that is below freezing. Only frost is a flight hazard.
notes.explanation: Dew poses no threat to a small UA; frost disrupts airflow, cutting lift and adding drag.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Dew and Frost”, p. 25

notes.front: Wind shear versus microburst: how are they related?
notes.back: Wind shear is any sudden change in wind over a small area; a microburst is its most severe low-level type.
notes.explanation: A microburst is a concentrated downdraft from convective precipitation.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Low-Level Wind Shear”, p. 24

notes.front: Normal atmosphere versus inversion: how does temperature change with height?
notes.back: Normally temperature falls as you climb; in an inversion it rises with height.
notes.explanation: An inversion layer is stable and traps haze, smoke and fog below it.
notes.source: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide (FAA-G-8082-22), ch. 3b, “Inversion”, p. 24
